Chapter 7. Listening to Understand, Not to Win.
After you’ve shared your own perspective, what comes next? It’s time to really listen. And I mean, listening not just to respond—or to win—but to understand.
That means setting aside the urge to defend your point, correct someone, or try to convince them you’re right. Instead, your main goal is to get where they’re coming from.
Deep listening is at the heart of great conversations. It’s how trust is built. And honestly, it’s how real solutions get discovered.
But listening well goes way beyond just hearing the words someone says. You want to tune in to their tone, their body language, and even the feelings that might be hiding underneath. It’s about being curious about their “story”—how they see the facts, and what those facts mean to them.
So, how do you actually do this? Here are a few techniques that make a huge difference:
First, ask open-ended questions. Instead of steering the conversation, invite them to share more. You might say, “Can you tell me more about what you were feeling?”
Next, try paraphrasing and reflecting. Put what you’ve heard into your own words to show you’re really listening—and check if you’ve got it right. Something like, “So you felt left out when I made that decision without you?”
Don’t forget to acknowledge emotions, even if they’re not spelled out. A simple, “It sounds like you were frustrated,” can go a long way.
And finally, suspend judgment. Resist the urge to jump in and evaluate or correct. Focus first on truly understanding.
Picture this: you’re at work, and a team member is upset about a new policy. Instead of explaining why the policy is great, imagine saying, “I hear that you’re concerned about how this will affect your workload. Can you walk me through your main worries?”
Just doing this helps your teammate feel seen and respected. And guess what? When people feel heard, they’re much more open to an honest conversation.
Listening like this doesn’t mean you have to agree with everything the other person says. It just means you’re willing to see things through their eyes, even for just a moment.
This simple act of empathy can totally change the mood of a conversation—turning conflict into real collaboration.
